title: Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak
hookLine: Sikhs and others mark Guru Nanak's birth with celebrations around the world

cards: At dusk, the strings of small lights along a gurdwara roof blink on. Clay lamps line a wall.
A procession moves through a city street, the Guru Granth Sahib carried on a decorated float, people sweeping the road clean in front of it, someone handing out sweets at the corner.
It looks like a festival of light, and it is one: Guru Nanak's gurpurab, the celebration of his birth. When the count reached a round number, the lights went up in Punjab and far beyond it.
Today: five hundred and fifty years of Nanak.

teach.b: First, the celebration. A gurpurab is a Guru's day. For Guru Nanak's, Sikhs hold an akhand path, an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, ending on the day itself.
There are nagar kirtans in the streets, langar for anyone, and lights in the evening. Second, why light.
Bhai Gurdas, in his first var, pictures Nanak's coming in a line people still quote: the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared, and light spread through the world.
The lamps on the gurdwara roof are that line, made visible. Third, what scholars notice.

The gurpurab is celebrated at the full moon of the month of Kartik, in autumn. Some early accounts of his life place his birth in a different month, in spring, and historians have discussed the difference.
Sikh practice keeps the celebration where it is, and both conversations go on side by side. Fourth, the round number. A count like five hundred and fifty is just arithmetic.

teach.h: WHAT PEOPLE DO WITH A NUMBER.
teach.b: What makes it matter is what people do with it.
When that count came, Sikhs and others marked it with kirtan, langar, lights and service, in villages and in cities across the world. The day wasn't about how long ago Nanak lived.
It was about whether his light is still spreading.

how: Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak's gurpurab with an akhand path ending on the day, nagar kirtan processions, langar and lights; round-number anniversaries are marked with larger gatherings in Punjab and around the world.

games.q: you're a historian, and the old accounts don't agree on the month of Guru Nanak's birth. what do Sikhs do with the celebration?
o: cancel it until the question is settled.
keep it in Kartik, while the discussion goes on.
games.why: Sikh practice keeps the gurpurab at the full moon of Kartik, and historians' discussion of the month goes on alongside it.

practice: In the procession, people sweep the street before the Guru Granth Sahib passes.
Bring to mind one person with a hard road just ahead, an exam, a hospital visit, a new job, a long goodbye, and with each breath out picture clearing one thing from it: a worry, a chore, a stone.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do.

wordCard.voice: Gurpurab. A Guru's day: Guru Nanak's birth, marked with akhand path, nagar kirtan, langar and lights around the world. Today's word.
